A.name: Directly observed
A.definition: A public source establishes the quantity, the supplier relationship or an actual disruption.

B.name: Strongly supported
B.definition: Several official sources establish the link, but the defence sector's own exposure cannot be observed.

C.name: Plausible
C.definition: A known technical use supports a possible exposure, with no evidence of the supply relationship.

D.name: Unknown
D.definition: Public information is not sufficient to describe the exposure.

covered_nations.quote: (2) Covered nation.-The term "covered nation" means- (A) the Democratic People's Republic of North Korea; (B) the People's Republic of China; (C) the Russian Federation; and (D) the Islamic Republic of Iran.

materials.use: Integrated circuits took 73% of US gallium consumption, and USGS says their uses “included defense applications, high-performance computers, and telecommunications equipment”. A Department of War release says of gallium and scandium together that “missile defense platforms, sensors, fighter aircraft, and hypersonic weapons all require these elements”.
materials.law: Added to the materials covered by 10 U.S.C. 4872, with effect from 18 December 2027. On the NATO list.
materials.supplier: No public source found names a supplier of gallium to a defence programme.
materials.substitutes: USGS: in many defence-related applications “no effective substitutes exist for GaAs and GaN”.
materials.stockpile: Not in the fiscal 2025 purchase plan.
materials.capacity: USGS lists primary production capacity of 120 tonnes a year outside China, 10 of it in Russia, against output of 9 tonnes. Rio Tinto says that if a trial succeeds it plans a demonstration plant in Quebec of up to 3.5 tonnes a year; it gives no start date (company statement).

materials.use: USGS lists US end uses, in descending order, as fibre optics, infrared optics, semiconductor applications and solar cells, and radiation detectors. A Department of War release names “infrared optics, night vision systems, surveillance windows, individual thermal weapon sights” and solar cells for military and civilian satellites.
materials.law: Added to the materials covered by 10 U.S.C. 4872, with effect from 18 December 2027. On the NATO list.
materials.supplier: No public source found names a supplier of germanium to a defence programme. For the US market as a whole, USGS estimates that imports of germanium metal fell by 67% in 2025 “owing to China's ban on germanium exports to the United States in 2024”.
materials.substitutes: USGS: chalcogenide glass has been used in place of germanium metal in infrared applications, and silicon in some electronics.
materials.stockpile: The fiscal 2025 plan listed 5,000 kilograms for possible sale and none for purchase. A recycling programme was expected to cover roughly 10% of US demand for purified germanium in 2023 (GAO).
materials.capacity: A US award is to expand one refiner's capacity for germanium metal “sevenfold to more than 20 metric tons annually”; no date is given.

materials.use: USGS gives US uses as metal products, including flame retardants, 49%, “antimonial lead and ammunition, 40%”, and nonmetal products 11%. A Department of Defense release says antimony trisulfide is used for “small arms and medium caliber cartridges, as well as many other missile and munition items”. A Department of War release says antimony metal and antimony trisulfide are used in primer production and case hardening.
materials.law: Not named in 10 U.S.C. 4872, in Public Law 119-60 or in the procurement regulation. Not on the NATO list. The table of shortfall materials in the 2021 White House review lists four application areas for antimony, none of them munitions. Antimony is in the stockpile purchase plan.
materials.supplier: GAO reports that in fiscal 2020 the Defense Logistics Agency funded the qualification of a US company sourcing antimony trisulfide from Mexico “to replace the only qualified source located in China”.
materials.supplier_scope: sole qualified source of one product; purchases not documented
materials.substitutes: USGS names substitutes for flame retardants, pigments and battery alloys. It does not mention ammunition. Recycling supplied 12% of US apparent consumption.
materials.stockpile: The fiscal 2025 plan allowed purchases of up to 700 tonnes.
materials.capacity: One US project reports work to keep it on track to start gold and antimony production in 2029 (company statement). USGS reports that one company began mining antimony in Montana in 2025 and that one US smelter made an estimated 700 tonnes from imported feedstock.

materials.use: USGS estimates that 60% of US tungsten use is in cemented carbide parts for cutting and wear. A Department of Defense release calls tungsten “a critical input for military-grade steel production, aerospace components, munitions, and ground vehicle armor”. The European Commission's research centre writes that it is required for armour-piercing ammunition.
materials.law: Tungsten metal powder and tungsten heavy alloy are covered by 10 U.S.C. 4872 now. From 1 January 2027 the statute also bars contracts for covered material mined, refined or separated in a named nation. The procurement regulation, last amended in 2024, has not yet been revised to that text. On the NATO list.
materials.supplier: No public source found names a supplier of tungsten to a defence programme.
materials.substitutes: USGS lists depleted uranium alloys or hardened steel as potential substitutes for tungsten alloys in armour-piercing projectiles, in some cases at higher cost or lower performance.
materials.stockpile: The fiscal 2025 plan allowed purchases of up to 2,041 tonnes of contained tungsten, and listed 499 tonnes of tungsten in ores for possible sale.
materials.capacity: Tungsten has not been mined commercially in the United States since 2015. A processing plant in South Korea received operating certificates on 17 September 2026 (company statement).

materials.use: USGS says the leading global use of rare earths is magnets. A Department of Defense release calls the magnets “essential components in the F-35, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles, and numerous other defense systems” and adds that these uses “represent a small part of the US commercial need”.
materials.law: Samarium-cobalt and neodymium-iron-boron magnets are covered by 10 U.S.C. 4872 now. From 1 January 2027 the statute also bars contracts for covered material mined, refined or separated in a named nation. The procurement regulation, last amended in 2024, has not yet been revised to that text. Rare earth elements are on the NATO list.
materials.supplier: GAO reports a defence official's statement that the F-35 programme “experienced 6-month production stoppages, in 2023 and 2024, when Chinese magnets were identified on the aircraft and had to be replaced”. GAO describes a pause in manufacturing of several months to identify alternative suppliers, and two national security waivers under which aircraft with the magnets were accepted.
materials.quantity: GAO, citing its 2016 report and Department of Defense estimates: total defence demand for rare earths “is less than 0.1 percent of the global demand”, and about 9,200 pounds are needed for each Virginia-class submarine. The figures are for rare earths and not for magnets.
materials.substitutes: USGS: substitutes “are available for many applications but generally are less effective”.
materials.stockpile: The fiscal 2025 plan allowed purchases of up to 450 tonnes of magnet block, 300 tonnes of neodymium-praseodymium oxide and 60 tonnes of samarium-cobalt alloy.
materials.capacity: One US maker states about 1,000 tonnes a year of finished magnets, ramping from late 2025, and an estimated 10,000 tonnes once a second plant is commissioned from 2028. Two other makers each state about 2,000 tonnes a year, one in the United States and one in Estonia (company statements). The Department of Defense assessed that new domestic sources for rare earths can take a decade or longer to establish (GAO).

germanium_supply_note: The USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries give no tonnage by country for germanium. They say germanium is “processed or recycled commercially in only a few countries, including the United States, Belgium, Canada, China, Germany, and Russia”.

visibility.quote: DOD officials recognize that they cannot use FPDS to determine where components of goods that DOD procures are produced.
they have collected country-of-origin information on less than 10 percent of all suppliers that provide components and raw materials for those parts
it has not yet determined how much total domestic capacity it needs to create in the long term to meet defense-related demand
costs anywhere from $250,000 to $3 million depending on the material
